title: Seed Development and Maturation on the Mother Plant
objective: Trace the development of a fertilized ovule into a mature cannabis dispersal unit and identify the maternal conditions that can affect seed quality.

terms.definition: Development of the embryo after fertilization.
Accumulation of storage reserves in the developing embryo and associated tissues.
Capacity to survive controlled water loss during late maturation.
The developmental state at which dry matter accumulation is substantially complete and the seed has acquired high potential quality.

coreScience: After successful pollination and fertilization, the ovule develops into the true seed while the ovary wall contributes to the surrounding fruit coat. In cannabis, the harvested unit is commonly called a seed but is botanically an achene-like one-seeded fruit. Inside it, the embryo differentiates into cotyledons, radicle, hypocotyl, and shoot-apex tissues while reserves accumulate for germination and early seedling growth.

Maturation is a sequence, not a color change. Developing units gain dry matter, acquire desiccation tolerance, reduce metabolic activity, and approach a quiescent dry state. Units on different branches or positions may not mature at exactly the same time. Exterior appearance may help sort a defined lot, but it is not itself a viability or vigor result; those endpoints require a stated test method.

Seed quality begins before harvest. Record parent identity, pollination date, seed position or harvest class, plant-health observations, maturity at harvest, and postharvest drying as potential explanatory variables. Their effects are genotype-, stage-, and system-dependent, so the record must not be treated as proof of causation. Handling after detachment cannot repair an embryo that was already immature or physically damaged.
cultivationRelevance: Treat seed production as a controlled crop with separate parent, pollination, maturation, harvest, and lot records. Harvesting mixed maturity classes into one unlabeled container hides the source of later germination problems.
Before storage, separate visibly damaged, incompletely filled, or contaminated units for evaluation. Visual grading can improve lot consistency, but a germination test is still needed.

Use staged harvest classes when seed maturation is visibly uneven. Keep early, intermediate, and apparently mature units physically separated, label their plant/branch positions, and test them independently. That creates evidence about whether later germination differences reflect position or maturity instead of averaging unlike material into one lot.

Maternal-plant stress records matter most when tied to timing. A drought, disease episode, heat event, nutrient disruption, or pollination problem during early embryogenesis may have a different consequence than the same event late in seed filling. Record when the event occurred relative to pollination and harvest rather than only noting that the mother plant was 'stressed'.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Record maternal and pollen parent IDs, source, generation, clone/seed-lot identifiers, and verification status. Link every harvested seed lot to both parents and preserve unknown or unverified pedigree elements explicitly.

Record date/time, branch or plant, flower stage, pollen batch, method, operator, containment, and whether a negative-control branch or plant was maintained. This anchors subsequent development to a known reproductive event.

Record major temperature/light events, irrigation or nutrition deviations, disease or pest pressure, physical injury, and maternal plant health with dates relative to pollination. Avoid retrospective causal claims when timing is unknown.

Record harvest date, plant and branch position, developmental class, exterior appearance, firmness, visible fill, mechanical damage, contamination, and separate container ID. Keep visibly different maturity classes separated for later testing.
Record drying conditions and duration, cleaning method, handling damage, final lot ID, storage package, storage entry date, and any period of uncontrolled humidity or temperature before storage.

After an appropriate storage/conditioning interval, record sample size, germination method, normal and abnormal seedlings, ungerminated/dead categories, timing metrics, and whether results differ among harvest classes or maternal positions.

misconceptions: Dark color guarantees maturity: Coat appearance is supportive evidence, not a direct test of embryo condition.
Every seed on one plant is equivalent: Position, pollination timing, injury, and maturation environment can produce within-plant variation.
Storage fixes immature seed: Cold, dry storage can slow deterioration; it cannot complete missing development after a poor harvest.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis-specific seed maturation timelines vary with genotype, pollination timing, maternal environment, branch/flower position, and production conditions. Exterior coat color, firmness, or days-after-pollination can support harvest decisions but do not directly establish embryo maturity, viability, or vigor. Maternal stress records are explanatory context rather than proof of causation unless matched comparisons or experiments isolate the factor.
